planting.note: Plant divisions in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; established clumps tolerate light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Hybridized by Hans P. Sass and introduced in 1940, Hesperus became the very first recipient of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1950. It bears clear orange-yellow, lightly ruffled flowers on tall, well-branched scapes that stay open later into the evening than most daytime-blooming cultivars. Plant divisions in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to sustain heavy flowering. Its garden toughness and reliable performance have kept it in commerce for more than eight decades.

planting.note: Set divisions in full sun with consistently moist, fertile soil; evergreen foliage performs best where winters are mild to moderate.

directions: Hybridized by Russell and honored with the Stout Silver Medal in 1951 after first receiving the Award of Merit in 1950, Painted Lady bears large, long-petaled orange-red polychrome blooms with pointed, slightly twisted segments that give the flower a spidery silhouette. Grow it in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun, since its evergreen foliage type prefers moderate winters. Divide clumps every few years to refresh bloom count and encourage a later rebloom flush. It remains one of the most historically significant orange daylilies from the mid-twentieth-century era of American hybridizing.

planting.note: Plant divisions in full sun and well-drained soil where winters provide a defined cold dormancy period.

directions: Bred by Fay and registered in 1957, Frances Fay earned the Stout Silver Medal in 1964 for its clear melon-yellow self-colored blooms, which stay open from early morning well into evening rather than closing at dusk like typical daylilies. The dormant foliage type benefits from a cold winter rest, so site divisions in full sun and well-drained soil in climates with distinct seasons. Divide clumps every three to four years once flowering declines to keep plantings vigorous. Its extended-bloom trait made it an influential parent in later breeding aimed at all-day flower display.

common_name: Becky Lynn Daylily (Rose Pink Stout Medal Winner)

planting.note: Grow divisions in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; lift and divide congested clumps every three to four years.

directions: Hybridized by Guidry in 1977, Becky Lynn advanced through the American Hemerocallis Society's award system to win the Stout Silver Medal in 1987. Its large rose-pink blooms carry a crisp white midrib above a yellow-green throat, opening early in the season with a reliable later rebloom flush. Grow divisions in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and lift and divide congested clumps every three to four years to sustain heavy bud count. Its bloom size, color clarity, and rebloom vigor made it a benchmark parent for later pink daylily breeding programs.

common_name: Ida's Magic Daylily (Amber Peach Stout Medal Winner)

planting.note: Plant divisions in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; evergreen foliage performs best where winters are mild to moderate.

directions: Hybridized by Ida Munson and registered in 1988, Ida's Magic earned the Stout Silver Medal in 2001 for its amber-peach blooms with wavy, gold-edged petals surrounding a broad green-yellow throat. This evergreen tetraploid opens its large flowers by day and reblooms across the season when grown in fertile, well-drained soil and full sun. Divide established clumps every three to four years to maintain flower count and vigor. It proved an especially influential parent plant, passing its broad throat pattern and ruffled edges to hundreds of later hybrids.

common_name: Rose F. Kennedy Daylily (Purple-Red Picotee Stout Medal Winner)

planting.note: Grow divisions in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil where winters provide a defined cold dormancy period.

directions: Hybridized by George A. Doorakian and introduced in 2007, Rose F. Kennedy earned the Stout Silver Medal in 2016 for its green-based blooms edged in a wide purple-red picotee band above a green throat. Its unusually broad, ruffled throat pattern influenced a new generation of diploid and tetraploid hybrids bred for wide, patterned flower centers. Plant divisions in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, dividing established clumps every three to four years to maintain bud count on the tall, well-branched scapes. This dormant-foliage cultivar blooms midseason and performs best where winters provide a defined cold rest.
